title: Salary or dividend: where the tax hides
assumptions: Illustrative example, not anyone's real numbers. Ontario resident; Ontario corporation (a CCPC).
The owner's income is already in the top federal and Ontario brackets, so each extra dollar is taxed at the top marginal rate.
The profit is active business income taxed at the small-business rate (within the $500,000 business limit; not shared with associated companies).
Everything is paid out in the same year; the dividend is non-eligible. Deferral (leaving money in the company) is a separate question.

Uses the rules in force for 2027: 33% federal and 13.16% Ontario top rates (rates aren't indexed; thresholds are, in November), Ontario surtax rates, the 2027 Ontario dividend credit (Bill 97) and the 11.2% corporate rate.
Quebec is different (QPP, its own rates and credits) and isn't covered.

The video's figures leave out payroll costs. Section D adds them with switches: CPP on salary (5.95% each for the owner and the company, 2026 rate, with the tax relief on the owner's share), EI (off when the owner has more than 40% of the votes), Ontario's Employer Health Tax (only above the $1 million exemption) and the Ontario Health Premium (flat at this income). Not modelled: the CPP2 band and the $3,500 exemption, the alternative minimum tax, and keeping money in the company.

review.note: Approved in chat, his words: "okay go proceed lets give it a shot" (after being asked for "go" and a sign-off on the facts). Recorded by Claude at his instruction; internal only.

The top federal personal rate is 33%.

claims.statement: A salary the company pays its owner to earn its business income is deductible to the company, so the company pays no corporate tax on it.

source.title: Income Tax Act s. 18(1)(a)
source.quote: In computing the income of a taxpayer from a business or property no deduction shall be made in respect of (a) an outlay or expense except to the extent that it was made or incurred by the taxpayer for the purpose of gaining or producing income from the business or property

supporting.title: Income Tax Act s. 67: deductible only to the extent reasonable in the circumstances

claims.note: Reasonableness (s. 67) applies; CRA generally doesn't question salaries paid to active owner-managers, but that is CRA's position, so the video says only that salary is deductible.

claims.statement: RRSP room grows by 18% of the previous year's earned income, up to a yearly dollar limit; salary is earned income and dividends are not.
claims.on_screen: RRSP ROOM: 18% OF LAST YEAR'S EARNED INCOME, UP TO THE YEARLY LIMIT

source.title: Income Tax Act s. 146(1) 'RRSP deduction limit' and 'earned income'
source.quote: the lesser of the RRSP dollar limit for the year and 18% of the taxpayer's earned income for the preceding taxation year … earned income … means … the taxpayer's income … from (i) an office or employment

claims.note: 'Dividend' doesn't appear in the earned-income definition. 2026 dollar limit $33,810 (CRA limits page) if shown.

claims.statement: CPP contributions (and so the CPP pension) are based on income from employment, so salary counts and dividends don't.

source.title: Canada Pension Plan s. 12(1)
source.quote: The amount of the contributory salary and wages of a person for a year is the person's income for the year from pensionable employment, computed in accordance with the Income Tax Act

claims.note: Salary also costs CPP contributions from both the company and the owner, up to the yearly ceiling; the worked example doesn't charge them.

claims.statement: Combined top marginal rate on salary, Ontario: 33% + 13.16% × (1 + 20% + 36%).
claims.spoken: about fifty-three and a half per cent

claims.statement: Salary route: the owner keeps $10,000 × (1 − 53.53%) ≈ $4,647.
Company's tax on small-business income, Ontario, from July 1, 2026: 9% + 2.2% = 11.2%.
Dividend route: the company's tax on the $10,000 first, $10,000 × 11.2% = $1,120.
claims.spoken: the company pays its tax first

claims.statement: Dividend route: what's left to pay out after corporate tax, $10,000 × (1 − 11.2%) = $8,880.
Top marginal rate on a non-eligible dividend, Ontario, 2027 credit: 1.15 × 33% − 0.15 × 9/13 + 1.15 × 13.16% × 1.56 − 0.15 × 15.2283% = 48.89% of the cash dividend.
claims.note: Order follows ON428: surtax on Ontario tax before the dividend credit (claim on-surtax-before-dtc).

calc.expr: round((1 + g) * fed - g * fdtc + (1 + g) * on * (1 + s20 + s36) - g * odtc, 7)

claims.statement: Dividend route: the owner keeps $8,880 × (1 − 48.89%) ≈ $4,539.
The salary route leaves about $108 more per $10,000 in this example.
$10,000 of salary adds $1,800 of RRSP room the next year (18%), if the owner is under the yearly limit.
Switch: does CPP apply to this $10,000 of salary? On (1) if the owner's salary for the year is below the CPP ceiling (for example, an owner who has been taking only dividends).
claims.note: Off (0) if the owner's salary is already above the CPP ceilings ($74,600 and $85,000 for 2026). The video's numbers equal this section with all switches off.

claims.statement: Switch: does Ontario's Employer Health Tax apply? On (1) only if the company's Ontario payroll is above its $1 million exemption (or it has no exemption: payroll over $5 million with associated employers).
claims.note: Most owner-managed companies are under the exemption, so it's off by default.

claims.statement: Switch: does EI apply? Off (0) when the owner controls more than 40% of the voting shares, because that employment isn't insurable.
CPP contribution rate on salary (base plus first additional), each for the employee and the employer: 5.95% (2026).

claims.statement: The salary the $10,000 can pay once the company's own payroll costs come out of it: $10,000 ÷ (1 + payroll costs).
The company's payroll costs (CPP, EHT, EI), deductible to the company.
The owner's own CPP contributions on that salary.
The owner's own EI premiums on that salary.

The owner's income tax on the salary at the top rate, less the deduction for enhanced CPP and the credits for base CPP and EI (at the lowest rates; Ontario's credit is also worth its surtax at this income).

claims.statement: Full picture, salary route: cash the owner keeps after payroll costs, CPP, EI and income tax.
Full picture: total CPP contributions (owner + company) that go toward the owner's CPP pension.
Full picture: salary cash minus dividend cash (a negative number means the dividend leaves more cash in hand; the salary's CPP contributions buy a pension instead).
